title: The Addition of Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) to IP
summary: Specifies adding Explicit Congestion Notification to IP and TCP, including its use of two bits in the IP header. Routers can signal congestion by marking packets instead of dropping them.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3168 adds Explicit Congestion Notification to IP and TCP. Instead of dropping packets when the network is congested, routers can mark them so senders slow down without losing data.

questions: how does ecn work in tcp
what are the ecn bits in the ip header
what is the difference between ect(0) and ect(1)
subtitle: Routers mark packets to signal congestion instead of dropping them, using two bits in the IP header and flags in TCP.

tldr.problem: TCP learns about congestion only when packets are lost, causing queues to build up even though routers can detect congestion earlier.
tldr.mechanism: Two bits in the IP header let routers set Congestion Experienced (CE) on ECN-capable packets. TCP negotiates ECN and uses ECE and CWR flags to echo the signal.
tldr.outcome: Senders react to a marked packet much like a dropped packet. RFC 3168 obsoletes RFC 2481 and has been updated by later RFCs.

today: RFC 3168 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoleted RFC 2481 and has been updated by RFC 4301, RFC 6040, RFC 8311 and RFC 9768.

sections.title: Why Mark Instead of Drop
sections.content:
TCP detects congestion only when packets are lost. Active queue management (AQM) can detect congestion before queues overflow, but without ECN it must signal by dropping packets. Dropping causes retransmissions and added delay, which hurts delay-sensitive traffic.

RFC 3168 adds Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) to IP and TCP. Routers can set the Congestion Experienced (CE) codepoint on ECN-capable packets instead of dropping them, letting the transport learn about congestion without loss. The design aims for incremental deployability and coexistence with existing congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: Rather than throwing packets away when the network is busy, routers can attach a mark telling senders to slow down. This avoids unnecessary retransmissions.

sections.title: Assumptions and Deployment
sections.content:
Section 3 sets out the design principles: because ECN is likely to be adopted gradually, it must accommodate incremental deployment without creating separate islands of ECN-capable and non-ECN-capable equipment, and it must co-exist with existing congestion control rather than replacing it.

Section 9 covers encapsulation: when IPv4 or IPv6 packets are carried inside IP or IPsec tunnels, the ECN field must be handled correctly, and the tunnel endpoints negotiate how to treat the field. Where a tunnel cannot preserve the field, some other signal is used. Sections 20 and 11.2 discuss why there are two ECT codepoints and how the ECN nonce lets the transport check that congestion signals are being reported honestly, though how TCP uses the nonce is not defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: ECN is meant to be switched on gradually, one part of the network at a time. If a router or a tunnel cannot carry the signal, the ordinary loss-based behavior still applies.

sections.title: ECN Bits in the IP Header
sections.content:
The ECN field uses two bits in the IP header (bits 6 and 7 of the TOS/Traffic Class octet), giving four codepoints: 00 Not-ECT, 01 ECT(1), 10 ECT(0), and 11 CE. The sender marks a packet as ECN-capable by setting ECT(0) or ECT(1); routers treat both ECT values the same and set CE to signal congestion.

When reassembling fragments, if any fragment had CE set, the reassembled packet gets CE (subject to specific rules). Pure ACKs must not indicate ECN-capability, and routers must not clear CE once set.
sections.plainLanguage: Two bits in each packet say either "not using ECN", "ECN-capable", or "congested". Routers can flip an ECN-capable packet to "congested" when busy.

sections.title: ECN in TCP
sections.content:
TCP uses two new flags in the TCP header: ECE (ECN-Echo) and CWR (Congestion Window Reduced). During connection setup, the endpoints negotiate ECN capability using the SYN and SYN-ACK flags. If both support ECN, data packets may carry ECT.

When a router sets CE on a packet received by the TCP receiver, the receiver sets ECE on subsequent ACKs to echo the congestion indication. When the sender receives an ACK with ECE set, it reduces its congestion window as it would for a dropped packet, and then sets CWR to acknowledge it. This provides a closed feedback loop without relying on packet loss.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP endpoints first agree to use ECN. If a packet arrives marked as congested, the receiver tells the sender to slow down by setting a flag in ACKs; the sender slows down and confirms it received the signal.

sections.title: Router Behavior and Non-compliance
sections.content:
Routers that use active queue management set the CE codepoint on ECN-capable packets that they would otherwise drop because of congestion, and leave Not-ECT packets alone. A router may still drop packets when it has to. ECN does not remove the need for the network to drop traffic under heavy load.

Sections 7 and 8 of the RFC discuss what happens when end nodes or nodes in the network do not follow the rules, including cases where packets are dropped rather than marked and where the CE indication is changed. The transport must treat a marked packet as a congestion signal at least as strong as a drop.
sections.plainLanguage: Busy routers mark instead of drop when they can. If some part of the network ignores the rules, the transport still slows down as it would for a lost packet.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Section 16 points to the security discussion in Sections 7, 8, 18 and 19. Sections 18 and 19 analyse what an attacker on the path could do to the ECN field: erase the congestion indication by turning CE back into ECT, falsely report congestion by setting CE with no congestion, disable ECN capability, or falsely claim it. For some of these, the effect is no worse than if the attacker had simply dropped the packet.

The RFC notes that a systematic erasure of CE by a downstream router can build queues upstream and cause unfairness between flows. It explains that the two ECT codepoints give the transport a way to detect such erasures, while the ECN nonce can expose dishonest reporting.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone on the path could hide or fake congestion signals. The RFC explains the harm each trick can do and how the two ECT codepoints help the transport catch some of them.
